Summary

Guidance from the Department for Education (DfE) and the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) on the safe, responsible and appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI) in children’s and adult social care in England.

It is intended to help local authorities, social care organisations and practitioners consider how AI may be used responsibly in practice.

It is not a technical guide and does not replace existing legal, regulatory or professional requirements.

DfE and DHSC recognise that, used appropriately, AI can support children’s and adult social care.

AI has the potential to:

support better outcomes

create more time for meaningful engagement with individuals and families

help practitioners develop a more informed and reflective understanding

identify gaps in information and help organisations make better use of information

support resource planning

strengthen decision-making and strategic oversight

Social care is fundamentally relationship-based. AI should always strengthen, not replace, human connection, professional judgement and accountability.

AI use raises ethical questions around:

accuracy and bias

transparency

consent

accountability

data protection

security risks

Local authorities and social care organisations should ensure AI use is governed appropriately. There should be clear guardrails in place, including:

acceptable use

data handling rules

training and supervision

monitoring and review

Responsibility and accountability remain with practitioners and their organisations.

Organisations should provide clarity on the AI tools that can be used to support practice, and the parameters that govern this use. No personal data should be entered into publicly available AI tools operating outside the organisation’s secure environment or enterprise agreements that protect onward sharing or use of data.

Decisions about whether or how to adopt AI remain with organisations and should be taken in line with their:

legal duties

local policies

data protection arrangements

professional standards and responsibilities

This guidance is intended to provide a foundation for DfE and DHSC to develop further resources (jointly where appropriate) to support ongoing responsible implementation, use and governance of AI tools in social care.

Who this publication is for

This guidance highlights universal themes applicable across organisations within children’s and adult social care. We understand that approaches will vary across local areas and organisations. The application of the guidance is at the discretion of the organisation.

This guidance is for:

frontline practitioners

supervisors

managers

digital and data teams

transformation teams

data protection officers

Caldicott guardians

procurement staff

other organisations providing social care and related services

The principles of this guidance will also apply to other organisations providing social care and related services.

Using this guidance

This guidance is intended to set out DfE and DHSC’s position on AI in social care and provide high-level guidance on its opportunities, risks and ethics.

We would recommend that the whole document is read and understood, but the following sections may help with specific queries:

how AI may support children’s and adult social care may help transformation or technical staff identify where AI could support practice

considerations for organisations and practitioners may be useful for practitioners and supervisors in understanding how to safely use AI in practice

considerations for the appropriate use of AI may also help managers and technical or transformation staff create the guardrails to support the safe use of AI

ethics, risks and challenges may help practitioners and supervisors understand the different risks and ethical dilemmas they may encounter when using AI

Using AI in social care: a quick guide for practitioners may help those new or unfamiliar with AI understand the basics

DfE has guidance on Generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education.

Main points

AI in this document means the tools used to:

generate, summarise, transcribe or organise information

support service improvement, communication, accessibility and analysis in support of children’s and adult social care practice

AI, used responsibly, can support social care practice by:

strengthening relationship-based and reflective practice

improving how information is used

testing assumptions

identifying gaps and reducing administrative burdens

strengthening services and supporting better decisions

AI is not infallible – it makes mistakes and practitioners should challenge AI outputs.

Responsibility and accountability remain with practitioners and their organisations. AI outputs should be treated as a first draft to be reviewed and amended before use.

Risks including bias, inaccuracy or hallucinations, privacy and security concerns, and automation bias (where AI outputs may be given undue weight by practitioners) should be identified and managed.

Practitioners should be able to clearly explain the AI tools being used, why, and what will be done with the outputs. This helps build trust and transparency.

Local authorities and social care organisations should have or be working to implement governance (including AI use policies), assurance and practical guardrails so AI is used safely, lawfully and appropriately.

Only platforms that are secure and data protection compliant should be used, and in line with organisational policies. Personal data should not be entered into AI tools that have not been approved by the organisation, as these are not secure.

The use of AI in social care should not jeopardise or impede the relational values of care, individual rights and dignities.

Lawful data processing

Article 5 of UK GDPR sets out seven main principles for data protection:

lawfulness

fairness and transparency

purpose limitation

data minimisation

accuracy

storage limitation

integrity and confidentiality (security)

accountability

These should be considered when implementing and adopting AI in children’s social care to provide the foundations for good data protection practice.

When processing personal data, whether AI is being used or not, a legal basis under Article 6 of the UK GDPR must be identified. Additionally, where that personal data is special category data (such as health data, racial or ethnic origin and sexual orientation), at least one of the conditions in Article 9 must be satisfied.

The common law duty of confidentiality (CLDC) must also be considered. More information is available from the duty of confidentiality.

The basic principle underlying the CLDC is that a person who receives information in confidence must not take unfair advantage of it or use or disclose it to the prejudice of the confider without consent.

In the absence of consent, the CLDC may be overridden on the basis of legal requirement, statutory power or overriding public interest.

Where automated processing is being used to make individual decisions, organisations must also consider whether the provisions in Section 4A of Chapter III of the UK GDPR apply. These provisions apply where automated processing is used to make a significant decision without meaningful human involvement in the taking of the decision.

Organisations should ensure that they have identified the relevant legal power and undertaken the analysis set out above when using AI and reflect this in their guidance and documentation as part of their implementation and governance approaches.

Ultimately, it is your responsibility to ensure you comply with all data protection legislation, and organisations may want to consider how they support practitioner compliance.

Trust and choice

Trust is fundamental to effective social care, and this should not be jeopardised by using AI or any other tool.

Organisations should support their frontline staff to understand the organisation’s policies on being transparent and what to do when people disagree to the use of AI when working with people who draw on care. This includes:

children

young people and families

people who may not be able to disagree themselves, for example during mental capacity assessments

This may include providing clear and accessible guidance and policies on transparency and the choices people have about the use of AI in practice and how to handle objections. This should be in line with data protection law, safeguarding responsibilities and local, organisational policy.

If practitioners understand their organisation’s policies on choice, and are able to explain the tools they use, this may help to:

build trust with individuals, children, young people, families and partner organisations

ensure alignment with data protection and safeguarding obligations

give individuals the opportunity to object to its use

There may be times when those families or individuals will not agree to AI being used in their care and support. They are within their rights to do so, and organisations should ensure that there are clear alternative processes in place for where individuals refuse permission to use AI.

When used with other organisations (for example in multi-agency meetings), it may be worth considering how agreement to use AI can be addressed through governance or at an organisational level. This is most likely to be relevant when using AI for recording or minuting meetings.

Practitioners should ensure that they adhere to different organisations’ policies on AI when working in partnership with them.

Transparency

Organisations should support transparency by ensuring staff understand what tools are in use, what they do, where they may be used, and how outputs should be used and reviewed. Where appropriate, organisations should also support practitioners to explain AI use clearly to children, families, carers, individuals and partner agencies.

This can be supported by ensuring practitioners:

understand, at a non-technical level, the AI tools that they are using, and how the output is generated

can explain how AI will be used in their practice, and outputs reviewed, to individuals, children, families and partner organisations where appropriate

can explain why AI is being used, understand where and when it can be used and the limitations and hard boundaries

understand when people should be informed and can disagree to the use of AI

are clear on how objections to AI use should be managed

understand and follow relevant organisational guidance

can feedback issues and challenges and share learning and practice with peers

are supported by organisational transparency about systems in use

Organisations may find the following resources useful for providing plain English guidance to staff around AI to support organisational transparency:

use of clear language

guidance and standards on plain English

Organisations may also want to consider how they can provide transparency more generally on the use of AI in social care, for example through accessible information for the public.

Buying and deploying tools appropriately

Organisations should use this policy paper, alongside wider advice and guidance, to create the conditions in which practitioners feel confident and supported to use AI:

appropriately

ethically

in the best interests of children, families and people who draw on care without diminishing their professional judgement and discretion

Organisations are responsible for creating the conditions for safe, appropriate and lawful use of AI. This should include:

procuring safe and secure tools

approving use cases for tools, and innovations

AI should not make autonomous decisions about assessment, risk, need, eligibility, safeguarding, care planning or intervention, or write unchecked content into case records.

1. Governance structure and accountability

A senior responsible owner is accountable for the organisation’s AI approach, with named operational, information governance, security and practice owners.

A defined governance forum has authority to approve, condition, reject, pause or withdraw AI tools and use cases.

Terms of reference set decision rights, membership, quorum, reporting arrangements, escalation routes and review frequency.

An AI policy defines approved, restricted and prohibited uses, required controls, practitioner accountability and exceptions.

A central register records every tool and use case, supplier, purpose, data used, risk rating, approvals, control owners, incidents and review dates. This should also include clarity on how risks, owners and mitigations or treatments are logged. The AI Risk Management toolkit has more information.

Organisational, managerial and practitioner responsibilities are clear, including who accepts residual risk.

2. Risk-based approval and assurance

Each use case is risk assessed in line with a risk appetite statement including a impact or likelihood score before procurement, pilot, deployment or material change.

Approval evidence covers intended benefit, non-AI alternatives, lawfulness, safeguarding, equality, ethics, privacy, security, accessibility, human oversight and business continuity.

Data protection, equality impact assessments, PSED (Public Sector Equality Duty) and Human Rights checks are completed where required and linked to the approval record.

Conditions of approval, acceptance thresholds, residual risks, review dates and stop or withdrawal criteria are documented.

Material changes to models, prompts, data, integrations, suppliers, terms or purpose trigger reassessment and reapproval.

3. Supplier and contract oversight

Due diligence tests supplier claims on functionality, limitations, accuracy, bias, security, data use and regulatory compliance.

Contracts cover data access, location, retention, deletion, reuse, model training, subcontractors, incidents, auditing, performance reporting and exit.

Suppliers must notify the organisation of material model, service, security or contractual changes.

Named contract owners monitor service levels, risks, incidents, updates, assurance evidence and corrective actions.

4. Operational oversight and human control

Approved workflows identify where human review, professional judgement and sign-off are mandatory.

Outputs entering records or informing practice are appropriately reviewed by the practitioner.

Managers use supervision and quality assurance to identify over-reliance, boundary breaches or inappropriate use.

Access controls, usage controls and technical restrictions support policy compliance.

Staff have clear routes for advice, challenge, incident reporting and protected escalation.

5. Audit and compliance assurance

An audit plan defines scope, frequency, sampling method, evidence requirements, responsible assurance function and reporting route.

Audits test whether only approved tools and uses are operating, required human review occurred, data rules were followed and records are accurate and complete.

Audit sampling is proportionate to risk and includes case records, outputs, user activity, exceptions, complaints and decisions influenced by AI.

Findings are reported to the governance forum and senior owner, with severity ratings, named actions, deadlines and follow-up verification.

Repeated, systemic or high-severity findings trigger escalation, increased sampling, control changes, suspension or withdrawal.

Independent assurance is considered for higher risk uses or where internal assurance is insufficient.

6. Monitoring, incidents and change control

The governance forum receives a regular oversight report covering usage, accuracy, corrections, bias, unequal impact, accessibility, security, incidents, complaints, benefits and control compliance.

Performance is reviewed across relevant groups, teams and settings to identify drift, exclusion or unequal outcomes.

Thresholds define when issues require investigation, corrective action, escalation, suspension or supplier remediation.

Incidents and near misses are logged, assessed, contained, investigated and reported through existing safeguarding, data, security and corporate risk routes.

Model drift, updates and changes in law, policy, practice or local context trigger reassessment.

Each tool has a scheduled review and explicit continuation, modification, suspension and withdrawal decisions.

7. Feedback, transparency and learning

Practitioners, managers, service users, and partner organisations have accessible routes to provide feedback, challenge use or raise concerns.

Organisations should consider how children, parents, carers and individuals who draw on care can inform the design and implementation of AI tools where they may affect people drawing on care and support.

Feedback, complaints, incidents, audit findings and evidence of benefit are logged, categorised, assigned and reviewed together by the governance forum.

Governance records show what was heard, the decision taken, action owner, timescale and, where no action is taken, the rationale.

Recording the tool on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standards (ATRS) has been considered – where relevant, this is best practice.

Learning informs approval conditions, controls, tools, contracts, policy, training, audit plans and monitoring thresholds.

Limitations and accountability are communicated transparently and a safe non-AI route is available where appropriate.
